posts.title: Ten minutes, slowly
posts.excerpt: Why ten slow minutes every day beat an hour on Sunday, and how to set the metronome.
posts.content:
Every new pupil hears the same advice in the first lesson: ten minutes a day, and slower than you think. Fingers learn by repetition, but only the repetitions you can play without a mistake.

Set the metronome to half the speed printed on the music. When a phrase is clean three times in a row, move it up two clicks. Stop while it still feels easy.

posts.title: Choosing a first piano
posts.excerpt: Upright, digital or a grand you inherited: what matters for the first two years.
posts.content:
For the first two years almost any piano will do, as long as it is in tune and the keys are full size and weighted. A good digital piano is better than a neglected upright.

Before buying a second-hand upright, ask a tuner to look inside. Bring your teacher to try it if you can; we never charge for the visit.

posts.title: What the pedal is for
posts.excerpt: The right pedal is not a volume knob. A short note for pupils who have just discovered it.
posts.content:
The right pedal lifts the dampers so the strings keep sounding. Used well it joins notes your hands cannot reach; used all the time it turns music into fog.

Practise every piece without pedal first. When you add it, change it just after the new harmony, never before, and listen to the bass.

posts.title: The winter recital order
posts.excerpt: Youngest first, teachers last, tea in the middle: how the afternoon is arranged.
posts.content:
The recital runs in the order of the lessons: First keys open the afternoon, then the young pianists, then the adults and diploma pupils after the interval.

The teachers close with a duet, chosen by the pupils from three suggestions. Last year it was a waltz; the year before, a march nobody admitted to choosing.

posts.title: Returning to the piano at fifty
posts.excerpt: Stiffer hands, better listening: what returning adults bring to the lesson.
posts.content:
Many of our adult pupils stopped at fourteen and came back at fifty. The hands are slower to begin with; the ears are much better than they were.

We start with pieces a little below the old level, rebuild the scales gently and let the repertoire grow from there. Most return to their old pieces within a year.

posts.title: Why we tune in October
posts.excerpt: Heating, humidity and the four tunings a year that keep the school's grand honest.
posts.content:
A piano moves with the seasons. When the heating comes on in autumn the soundboard dries and the pitch drops, so the school's pianos are tuned in the first week of October.

At home, once a year is enough. Keep the piano away from the radiator and the window, and close the lid when you are not playing.
